q: Where is the V1 electrode placed?
choices: Fifth intercostal space, left midclavicular line
Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
Fifth intercostal space, right midaxillary line
why: V1 sits in the fourth intercostal space at the right sternal border. The fourth intercostal space at the LEFT sternal border is V2, not V1.

q: A technician is locating V2. Which position is correct?
choices: Fourth intercostal space, left sternal border
Fourth intercostal space, right sternal border
Third intercostal space, left sternal border
Fifth intercostal space, left sternal border
why: V2 is the fourth intercostal space at the left sternal border, directly across from V1. The right sternal border position is V1.

q: V4 is correctly positioned at the:
choices: Fifth intercostal space, anterior axillary line
why: V4 goes in the fifth intercostal space at the midclavicular line. The fifth space at the anterior axillary line is V5.

q: Why is V4 usually applied before V3?
choices: V3 is placed midway between V2 and V4, so V4 must exist first
V4 anchors the limb lead calculation
V3 is optional on a routine 12-lead
why: V3 has no independent landmark; it is defined as the midpoint between V2 and V4, so V4 must be placed first. V3 is never optional on a standard 12-lead.

q: V6 is placed in the fifth intercostal space at which line?
why: V6 is at the midaxillary line, level with V4 and V5. The anterior axillary line is V5's landmark.

q: A technician palpates downward from the angle of Louis to find a landmark. This maneuver locates the:
choices: Second rib and therefore the second intercostal space, counted down to the fourth
why: The angle of Louis marks the second rib; the space just below it is the second intercostal space and the technician counts down to the fourth for V1 and V2. The xiphoid is not a reliable rib-counting landmark.

q: Limb electrodes should be placed on:
choices: Fleshy, non-bony areas of the upper arms and lower legs
The wrists and ankles over bone for stability
The upper chest for all patients
why: Fleshy muscular areas give better contact and less artifact than bony prominences. Placing electrodes over bone increases noise and poor adhesion.

q: A woman has large pendulous breasts. Where should V4 and V5 be applied?
choices: On top of the breast tissue
On the upper chest above the breast
Under the breast, on the chest wall at the correct intercostal space
why: Precordial electrodes go under the breast directly on the chest wall so the anatomic position is preserved; placing them on top of breast tissue attenuates and distorts voltages. Leads are never simply omitted.

q: A patient has a right arm amputation above the elbow. The technician should:
choices: Place the right arm electrode on the right shoulder or upper right torso and document it
Place the electrode on the left arm with the left arm electrode
why: The electrode moves proximally to the nearest available site on the same side and the deviation is documented. Placing two limb electrodes on one limb would invalidate the Einthoven triangle.

q: Which statement about lead II is correct?
choices: It is an augmented unipolar lead
It is a bipolar limb lead viewing the inferior wall
It views the high lateral wall
why: Lead II is bipolar (right arm to left leg) and, with III and aVF, views the inferior wall. Augmented leads are aVR, aVL, and aVF.

q: Einthoven law states that:
why: The sum of the voltages in leads I and III equals lead II. I + II = III is a common distractor but reverses the relationship.

q: Which leads view the septal wall of the left ventricle?
why: V1 and V2 sit over the interventricular septum. II, III, and aVF view the inferior wall.

q: Which group of leads views the lateral wall?
why: I, aVL, V5, and V6 are the lateral leads. V1 through V3 are septal and anterior.

q: ST elevation in II, III, and aVF suggests injury to which wall?
why: II, III, and aVF are the inferior leads, supplied usually by the right coronary artery. Anterior changes would appear in V3 and V4.

q: A patient with an inferior wall MI becomes hypotensive. The physician asks for right-sided leads. Which lead is most important?
why: V4R is the single most useful right-sided lead for detecting right ventricular infarction. V7 and V9 are posterior leads, not right-sided.

q: Posterior leads V7, V8, and V9 are placed:
choices: In the second intercostal space bilaterally
On the left posterior chest at the level of V6, at posterior axillary line, midscapular line, and left border of the spine
why: V7 through V9 continue the horizontal V6 plane around the left posterior chest. They are not placed over the scapular spines.

q: For right-sided chest leads, the electrodes are placed:
choices: In the same positions but one space higher
In mirror-image positions on the right side of the chest
why: Right-sided leads mirror the standard precordial positions across the sternum. Raising the leads one interspace is not the technique.

q: In a 3-lead monitoring setup, the white electrode is placed:
why: White on right, under the right clavicle. Black (smoke) goes on the left below the clavicle, over the red (fire) lower left.

q: The mnemonic smoke over fire means:
choices: Black electrode above the red electrode on the left side
Red above black on the right side
White above green on the left
why: Smoke (black) sits above fire (red) on the patient's left. Brown is the chest electrode placed in the middle in a 5-lead setup.

q: In a 5-lead system, the brown electrode is placed:
choices: In the V1 position, fourth intercostal space right sternal border
why: Brown is the chest lead and is typically placed at V1. The right and left lower positions belong to green and red.

q: Before applying electrodes to a diaphoretic patient with hairy skin, the technician should first:
choices: Clip the hair, wipe the skin with alcohol, let it dry, and gently abrade
Apply extra gel over the hair
Apply electrodes over the hair and tape them down
why: Hair removal, oil removal with alcohol, drying, and gentle abrasion all lower skin impedance. Lotion increases impedance and prevents adhesion.

q: An electrode package is opened and the gel appears dry and cracked. The technician should:
choices: Use it anyway and increase the gain
Discard it and open fresh, unexpired electrodes
why: Dried or expired gel raises impedance and produces artifact or lead-off; fresh electrodes are required. Raising gain amplifies the noise along with the signal.

q: A tracing shows a slow, drifting up-and-down movement of the isoelectric line. This is:
why: Slow drift of the baseline is wandering baseline, commonly from patient movement, breathing, or loose electrodes. AC interference is fast, uniform, small spikes.

q: Which action best corrects wandering baseline caused by respiration?
choices: Increase the paper speed to 50 mm/sec
Ask the patient to breathe normally and hold still, and check electrode adhesion
why: Wandering baseline from breathing and loose contact is fixed by securing electrodes and limiting motion. The AC filter addresses 60-cycle interference, a different artifact.

q: A tracing shows fuzzy, irregular, rapid spikes of varying height throughout. The most likely cause is:
why: Irregular, jagged, variable deflections indicate muscle tremor from tension, shivering, or movement. AC interference is regular and uniform, not irregular.

q: AC 60-cycle interference appears on the tracing as:
choices: Uniform, small, rapid spikes at a constant rate across the baseline
Irregular coarse waves of varying amplitude
why: Alternating current interference produces perfectly regular fine spikes. A flat line suggests a lead-off or disconnected wire instead.

q: Which action is the best first step to eliminate AC interference?
choices: Unplug or move nearby electrical equipment and ensure lead wires are not crossing power cords
why: AC interference originates from nearby powered equipment and cords, so removing the source is the first fix. Changing paper speed does not affect electrical interference.

q: A patient with Parkinson disease produces continuous tremor artifact. The best option is:
choices: Position the limbs comfortably on supports, move limb electrodes more proximally, and apply the muscle filter
Ask the patient to hold their breath for 60 seconds
why: Supported limbs, more proximal electrode placement, and the muscle artifact filter reduce involuntary tremor artifact. Removing limb leads would make the 12-lead impossible.

q: A flat line appears only in lead III while other leads are normal. The most likely cause is:
choices: A loose or disconnected electrode or broken lead wire on that limb
why: A single interrupted or flat lead points to a mechanical problem with that electrode or wire, not the patient. True asystole would flatten all leads simultaneously.

q: Lead I shows a negative P wave and negative QRS while aVR shows upright complexes. The technician should suspect:
choices: Right arm and left arm electrode reversal
why: RA and LA reversal inverts lead I and makes aVR look like a normal lead. It is corrected by re-placing electrodes and repeating, not reported as a normal variant.

q: A monitored tracing shows almost no amplitude in leads II, III, and aVF while lead I looks normal. The most likely technical cause is:
choices: Dry electrode gel on the chest leads
Reversal of the left leg and right leg electrodes
why: LL and RL reversal produces a nearly flat lead II because the two electrodes are electrically similar. Paper speed changes width, not amplitude.

q: The standard paper speed for a routine 12-lead EKG is:
why: 25 mm/sec is the universal standard. 50 mm/sec is reserved for very fast rates or crowded complexes and doubles the apparent width.

q: On standard paper, one small box horizontally represents:
why: At 25 mm/sec, each 1 mm small box equals 0.04 second. 0.20 second is one large box of five small boxes.

q: One large box on standard EKG paper represents:
why: Five small boxes at 0.04 second each equal 0.20 second. 0.04 second is one small box.

q: With normal standardization, a 10 mm deflection equals:
why: Standardization is 10 mm per 1 millivolt. Half standardization would make 5 mm equal 1 mV.

q: QRS complexes are so tall they overlap adjacent leads. The technician should:
choices: Switch to half standardization, 5 mm/mV, and mark the tracing
why: Half standardization halves amplitude so complexes fit, and it must be documented on the tracing. Changing paper speed alters duration, not height.

q: Double standardization is set at:
why: Double standardization doubles the deflection to 20 mm per mV, used when complexes are very small. 5 mm/mV is half standardization.

q: The standardization mark on a correctly calibrated tracing should be:
why: The calibration pulse is a 10 mm by 0.20 second rectangle confirming 1 mV equals 10 mm. A 5 mm mark indicates half standardization.

q: If the machine is accidentally left at half standardization, the resulting tracing will:
choices: Show artificially small amplitudes that could mask hypertrophy
why: Half standardization halves all voltages, which can hide true voltage criteria; timing is unaffected. Rate and intervals depend on paper speed, not gain.

q: How many large boxes span 6 seconds at 25 mm/sec?
why: Each large box is 0.20 second, so 30 large boxes equal 6 seconds; 15 large boxes equal 3 seconds. Rate is estimated by counting complexes in the 6-second strip and multiplying by 10.

q: A patient's complexes are crowded together at a rate of 190/min. The technician may:
choices: Increase paper speed to 50 mm/sec and document the change
why: Doubling paper speed spreads the complexes so waveforms can be measured, and the change must be noted. Gain changes affect height, not spacing.

q: The muscle or artifact filter is most appropriately used when:
choices: Tremor artifact persists after repositioning and reassurance
why: The filter is a last step after mechanical and patient-related fixes, because filtering can also alter true waveform detail. It does nothing for amplitude problems.

q: Before handing a completed tracing to the provider, the technician should:
choices: Review it for artifact, correct lead placement, proper standardization, and complete patient identification
Interpret the rhythm and write a diagnosis
Send it without review to save time
why: Quality review and correct labeling are technician responsibilities. Interpreting and diagnosing are outside the CET scope of practice.

q: A tracing must be repeated when:
choices: The patient has an abnormal rhythm
Artifact obscures the baseline or leads were misplaced
why: An uninterpretable or incorrectly acquired tracing must be repeated. An abnormal but clean rhythm is real data and should be reported, not repeated.

q: A patient with severe dyspnea cannot lie flat for the EKG. The technician should:
choices: Place the patient in semi-Fowler position and document the position on the tracing
why: Semi-Fowler is acceptable when supine is not tolerated, but the deviation must be documented because position changes axis and amplitude. Forcing a supine position risks harm.

q: The standard position for a routine 12-lead EKG is:
choices: Supine with arms relaxed at the sides and legs uncrossed
why: Supine with relaxed limbs minimizes muscle artifact. Crossed legs and tensed arms introduce somatic tremor.

q: Which instruction should be given to the patient immediately before recording?
choices: Relax, remain still, and do not talk during the recording
Cough at the start of each lead
Lift the head to check the electrodes
why: Stillness and silence prevent somatic and baseline artifact. Deep breathing causes baseline sway.

q: A patient has a chest tube dressing covering the V3 position. The technician should:
choices: Place V3 as close as safely possible to the correct site, avoiding the dressing, and document the deviation
Skip V3 and report a 11-lead EKG
why: The electrode is shifted minimally and the deviation documented; sterile dressings are never removed by the technician. Omitting the lead yields an incomplete study.

q: When a patient has an implanted pacemaker generator under the left clavicle, the technician should:
choices: Place limb electrodes on the abdomen
Avoid placing electrodes directly over the generator site
why: Electrodes are kept off the generator pocket to avoid discomfort and distortion; the pacemaker is never manipulated. Skipping leads is not acceptable.

q: Pediatric 12-lead EKGs commonly add which lead?
why: V4R is routinely added in pediatric tracings because of right ventricular dominance in children. V7 through V9 are posterior leads used for suspected posterior infarction.

q: A Holter monitor is typically worn for:
why: Standard continuous Holter recording is 24 to 48 hours. Event or mobile telemetry monitors cover 30 days for infrequent symptoms.

q: A patient being fitted for a Holter monitor should be instructed to:
choices: Shower daily with the monitor on
Keep a diary of activities and symptoms with times
why: The diary lets the physician correlate symptoms and activity with recorded rhythm. Showering is not permitted because water loosens electrodes and can damage the recorder.

q: Which patient statement indicates a need for further Holter teaching?
choices: I will write down when I feel dizzy
I will take the monitor off before my shower tomorrow
I will keep the lead wires tucked under my shirt
why: Removing the monitor interrupts continuous recording and invalidates the study; the patient should sponge bathe instead. The other statements are correct practice.

q: An event monitor differs from a Holter monitor because it:
choices: Records intermittently over weeks, often activated by the patient during symptoms
why: Event and loop recorders capture infrequent symptoms over up to 30 days rather than recording continuously for a day or two. They are outpatient devices.

q: Mobile cardiac telemetry is distinguished by:
choices: Recording only when the patient presses a button
Producing a printed strip at home
Automatic detection and wireless transmission of arrhythmias to a monitoring center in near real time
why: Mobile cardiac telemetry auto-detects and transmits events continuously. An implanted device is an insertable loop recorder, a different technology.

q: Which is an absolute contraindication to exercise stress testing?
choices: Acute myocardial infarction within the last two days
why: Acute MI, unstable angina, severe aortic stenosis, and uncontrolled arrhythmias are absolute contraindications. Stable angina is a common indication for testing, not a contraindication.

q: Which patient should not proceed with a treadmill stress test?
choices: A patient with a remote MI five years ago
A patient with severe symptomatic aortic stenosis
A patient taking a beta blocker
A patient with a history of asthma
why: Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis is an absolute contraindication because exertion can cause syncope or sudden death. A remote MI is not a contraindication.

q: Pre-test instructions for a stress test should include:
choices: No food, caffeine, or tobacco for several hours before, and wear comfortable walking shoes
Eat a large meal for energy
Drink strong coffee to raise heart rate
why: Fasting and avoiding caffeine and nicotine prevent nausea and heart rate distortion; walking shoes are needed for treadmill safety. Caffeine interferes with the test and with pharmacologic agents.

q: Informed consent for a stress test must be:
choices: Obtained verbally by the technician only
Waived because the test is noninvasive
Signed by the patient after the physician explains risks and benefits
why: The physician explains risks and benefits and the patient signs before the test starts. The test carries real risk, so consent is never waived.

q: In the Bruce protocol, each stage lasts:
why: Bruce protocol stages are 3 minutes each, with speed and grade increasing at every stage. Shorter stages would not allow a steady-state response.

q: A 60-year-old is having a stress test. The predicted maximum heart rate is:
why: Maximum predicted heart rate is 220 minus age, so 220 minus 60 equals 160/min. 136/min would be the 85 percent target, not the maximum.

q: A 40-year-old patient's 85 percent target heart rate for a stress test is approximately:
why: 220 minus 40 equals 180, and 85 percent of 180 is 153/min. 180/min is the maximum predicted rate, not the target.

q: During stress testing, limb electrodes are moved to the torso because:
choices: Arm and leg motion during walking would create unacceptable artifact
The limbs cannot conduct during exercise
why: Torso placement eliminates limb motion artifact while walking. It actually alters amplitude and axis slightly, which is why torso tracings are labeled as such.

q: During each stage of a stress test the technician should record:
choices: Blood pressure, heart rate, rhythm, and patient symptoms
why: Serial blood pressure, rate, rhythm, and symptoms are monitored each stage to detect a dangerous response. Heart rate alone would miss a falling systolic pressure.

q: During stage 3 the patient's systolic blood pressure falls from 150 to 132 mmHg. The technician should:
choices: Do nothing since diastolic is unchanged
Notify the physician immediately, as a drop of 10 mmHg or more is an indication to stop
why: A sustained fall in systolic pressure of 10 mmHg or more with increasing workload signals ischemia or a failing cardiac output and is an absolute indication to terminate. Continuing raises the risk of a serious event.

q: Which finding is an absolute indication to stop a stress test?
choices: Heart rate reaching 70 percent of predicted maximum
A rise in systolic pressure to 170 mmHg
why: Sustained VT, ST elevation, severe chest pain, dizziness, a falling systolic pressure, or patient request all require immediate termination. A normal rise in systolic pressure with exercise is expected.

q: A patient says I want to stop during stage 2 but has no other findings. The technician should:
choices: Encourage the patient to reach target rate first
Stop the test, because patient request is a valid reason to terminate
why: Patient request alone terminates the test; no patient is compelled to continue. Pushing on despite a request is both unsafe and unethical.

q: After a stress test ends, monitoring should continue:
choices: Only until the patient leaves the room
Through a recovery period until heart rate, blood pressure, and EKG return toward baseline
why: Many ischemic changes and arrhythmias appear in recovery, so monitoring continues until values approach baseline. Ending monitoring at the treadmill stop can miss these events.

q: Pharmacologic stress testing is chosen primarily when the patient:
choices: Cannot exercise adequately due to arthritis, deconditioning, or neurologic limits
why: Pharmacologic agents simulate exercise stress for patients who cannot walk sufficiently. A normal resting EKG is not itself a reason to avoid the treadmill.

q: Adenosine and regadenoson produce stress by:
choices: Causing coronary vasodilation that reveals relative perfusion differences
why: These agents are vasodilators that unmask perfusion mismatch between normal and stenotic vessels. Dobutamine, not adenosine, works by increasing contractility and rate.

q: Dobutamine is used in pharmacologic stress testing because it:
choices: Increases heart rate and myocardial contractility, mimicking exercise
why: Dobutamine raises rate, contractility, and oxygen demand much as exercise does. Coronary vasodilation alone describes adenosine and regadenoson.

q: A patient scheduled for adenosine stress testing reports drinking two cups of coffee this morning. The technician should:
choices: Report it, because caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and can invalidate the test
why: Caffeine and other methylxanthines antagonize adenosine receptors and blunt the response, so the test is usually rescheduled. Increasing the dose is not the technician's decision and is unsafe.

q: Echocardiography differs from electrocardiography in that it:
choices: Uses ultrasound to image cardiac structure, wall motion, and valve function
why: Echo is an ultrasound image of anatomy and mechanical function; the EKG records electrical activity only. A normal EKG does not rule out structural disease.

q: A telemetry monitor alarms with a flat line, but the patient is sitting up talking. The technician should first:
choices: Check the electrodes and lead wires for a lead-off or disconnection
why: An alert, conversant patient rules out asystole, so the cause is a lead-off or detached wire. Silencing the alarm without correcting the cause is unsafe practice.

q: Alarm limits on a cardiac monitor should be:
choices: Set appropriately for the individual patient's condition and prescribed parameters
Always set at 40 and 200/min for everyone
why: Limits are individualized so real events are caught without constant false alarms. Disabling alarms is a serious safety violation.

q: The monitor shows frequent false high-rate alarms with normal-appearing rhythm. A likely cause is:
choices: Tall T waves being double counted by the monitor
why: Large T waves can be counted as additional QRS complexes, doubling the displayed rate; selecting a lead with a taller QRS relative to T corrects it. Paper speed does not affect monitor rate counting.

q: When mounting or labeling a 12-lead tracing, the technician must include:
choices: Patient name, identification number, date, time, and technician initials
why: Complete identifying data makes the tracing a valid legal record. Interpretation is the provider's responsibility, not the technician's.

q: A technician notices that V5 and V6 were transposed after the tracing printed. The correct action is:
choices: Report it as a lateral infarct
Correct the electrode positions and repeat the tracing, documenting the correction
Ignore it since the leads are adjacent
why: Misplaced precordial leads distort R wave progression and must be corrected and re-recorded. Hand relabeling falsifies the record.

q: Poor R wave progression appears across the precordial leads on an otherwise clean tracing. A common technical cause is:
choices: Incorrect vertical placement of the chest electrodes, such as placing them an interspace too high
why: Chest electrodes placed too high shift R wave transition and can mimic anterior infarction. 25 mm/sec and 10 mm/mV are the correct standard settings.

q: Which action reduces the chance of skin irritation from electrodes on a fragile elderly patient?
choices: Scrub the skin vigorously with abrasive pads
Leave the electrodes on for several days
Use fresh hypoallergenic electrodes and remove them gently after the tracing
Apply alcohol after the electrode is placed
why: Hypoallergenic electrodes and gentle removal protect fragile skin. Vigorous abrasion can tear thin skin.

q: A limb electrode is accidentally placed on the right thigh rather than the left leg while the other is on the left arm. The result is:
choices: Distorted lead relationships because the Einthoven triangle is altered
why: The limb electrodes define the triangle used to derive leads I, II, III and the augmented leads, so misplacement distorts axis and morphology. Electrode location does not change the true heart rate.

q: A 5-year-old is scheduled for an EKG and is frightened. The best approach is:
choices: Explain the procedure in simple terms, allow a caregiver present, and use pediatric-sized electrodes
Perform it while the child cries
why: Simple explanation, caregiver presence, and correctly sized electrodes reduce motion artifact and fear. A crying, struggling child produces an uninterpretable tracing.

q: Aside from V4R, pediatric tracings often require:
choices: Smaller electrodes placed in anatomically proportional positions
Doubling paper speed to 50 mm/sec routinely
why: Smaller electrodes keep the precordial positions from overlapping on a small chest. Paper speed remains 25 mm/sec unless rates are extremely fast.

q: An EKG machine has not been checked for calibration in a year. The technician should:
choices: Continue using it if tracings look normal
Follow facility policy for scheduled calibration and preventive maintenance and remove it from use if out of specification
Recalibrate it personally with household tools
why: Scheduled calibration and biomedical maintenance ensure accurate amplitude and timing. Adjusting gain does not correct a miscalibrated machine and would falsify voltages.

q: A lead wire has a visibly cracked insulation and its lead produces intermittent interrupted baseline. The technician should:
choices: Remove the damaged cable from service and replace it
Use it only for limb leads
why: A broken conductor causes intermittent signal loss and cannot be reliably repaired with tape. Filtering hides the artifact without fixing the defect.

q: Lead aVR normally shows:
choices: An upright QRS and upright P wave
A predominantly negative deflection because it views the heart from the right shoulder
The tallest R wave of any lead
why: aVR points away from the main electrical vector, so complexes are normally negative. Upright complexes in aVR suggest arm lead reversal or dextrocardia.

q: Which leads are the augmented unipolar limb leads?
why: aVR, aVL, and aVF are augmented unipolar leads. I, II, and III are the bipolar standard limb leads.

q: How many electrodes are applied to record a standard 12-lead EKG?
why: Ten electrodes, four limb and six chest, generate the twelve views. The number twelve refers to the leads or views, not the electrodes.

q: The hexaxial reference system is derived from:
choices: The six limb leads arranged around the frontal plane
why: The six frontal plane limb leads form the hexaxial diagram used for axis determination. The precordial leads define the horizontal plane instead.

q: A patient has a full arm cast on the left arm. The best action is:
choices: Place the left arm electrode on the left shoulder or upper torso above the cast and document it
Place both arm electrodes on the right arm
why: Move the electrode proximally to exposed skin on the same limb and document the deviation. Electrodes cannot conduct through casting material.

q: A patient has extensive burns over the left chest. The technician should:
choices: Place electrodes over the burn with extra gel
Place electrodes as near to correct position as intact skin allows, avoid the wound, and document the deviation
Use limb leads only and call it a 12-lead
why: Intact skin is used, the wound is protected, and the deviation is documented so the reader can interpret accordingly. Placing electrodes on burned tissue risks infection and pain.

q: A telemetry patient is ambulating and the rhythm becomes unreadable with wide erratic deflections. The technician should first:
choices: Assess the patient and check electrode adhesion and lead wire slack
Print the strip as a new arrhythmia
why: Motion artifact from ambulation is corrected by checking the patient and the electrode connections. Documenting artifact as an arrhythmia creates a false record.

q: To minimize artifact, telemetry electrodes should be placed:
choices: Over the sternum for all leads
Over flat bony areas away from large muscle masses and away from breast tissue
why: Flatter, less muscular sites reduce somatic artifact and keep electrodes stable. Placing electrodes on large moving muscles maximizes artifact.

q: How often should telemetry electrodes generally be changed?
choices: Every 24 to 48 hours or when signal quality declines or the gel dries
Only when the patient is discharged
why: Daily replacement or replacement when the signal degrades keeps gel moist and impedance low. Leaving electrodes until discharge leads to dried gel and artifact.

q: A tracing is acquired at 25 mm/sec and the technician counts 4 QRS complexes in 30 large boxes. The heart rate is approximately:
why: Thirty large boxes equal 6 seconds, so 4 complexes times 10 equals 40/min. Multiplying by 5 would apply to a 3-second, 15-large-box strip.

q: On an EKG, one small box vertically represents:
why: At standard gain, 10 mm equals 1 mV, so each 1 mm small box equals 0.1 mV. 0.04 is the time value of a small box in seconds, not a voltage.

q: A technician is told to obtain a rhythm strip. This usually means:
choices: A continuous recording of a single monitoring lead, most often lead II
why: A rhythm strip is one continuous lead, typically lead II because P waves are well seen. A 12-lead is a different, multi-view study.

q: When the technician notices ST elevation on a resting 12-lead of a patient with chest pain, the appropriate action is:
choices: Reassure the patient it is artifact
Repeat the EKG three times before telling anyone
Notify the provider immediately and stay with the patient
File the tracing in the chart for the next rounds
why: Suspected acute injury is reported to the licensed provider without delay while the patient is monitored. Delaying for repeat tracings or routine filing risks a fatal delay in treatment.

q: The primary purpose of the standardization mark printed at the beginning of a tracing is to:
choices: Verify that the machine is recording 1 mV as 10 mm so amplitudes can be measured accurately
why: The calibration pulse documents the gain used so voltages on the tracing are interpretable. Patient identity is established by the labeling, not the calibration mark.

q: Lead placement documentation for a nonstandard tracing should be recorded:
choices: Verbally to the next technician only
Not at all if the tracing looks good
In the patient record and directly on the tracing
Only if the provider requests it
why: Written notation on the tracing and in the record tells the interpreter that positions deviated, preventing misdiagnosis. Verbal handoff is not a durable legal record.

q: A patient asks the technician what the EKG shows. The best response is:
choices: Give a rough interpretation to ease anxiety
State that the provider will review and discuss the results, and offer to answer questions about the procedure
Show the patient the tracing and point out abnormalities
why: Interpreting or reassuring about findings exceeds the CET scope of practice; explaining the procedure does not. Offering an informal reading can cause harm if wrong.

q: A technician must perform an EKG on a patient wearing a transdermal medication patch at the V2 position. The appropriate action is:
choices: Place the electrode on top of the patch
Ask the patient to hold the patch aside
Follow policy to have the patch relocated or removed per the nurse, then place V2 correctly and document
why: The electrode must contact skin at the anatomically correct spot, and patch removal or relocation is coordinated with nursing so the medication dose is tracked. Placing an electrode on the patch prevents proper conduction.
